batch_note: Yes, two templates predict the key across items. (1) Eight 'which finding' items (A-01, A-03, B-01, B-02, C-01, C-03, D-01, D-02) are built on two sites that pull the accounts apart. In seven of them (all but D-02) the options are two reversed pairs: one pair is the pattern the passage says 'both accounts fit' plus its negation, and the other is the two passage-named dissociating sites, both ways. The key is always the site-pair option in the direction of the named hypothesis, so a test-wise student strikes two options without reasoning on every one. D-02 breaks the template by comparing across rivers and plays genuinely hard. (2) Six table items (A-04, A-06, C-04, C-05, D-05, D-06) follow 'X beat every member of class Y'. The key is always the strongest member of Y, with one or two off-class options and an extreme value as distractors, so 'the closest in-class competitor' predicts the key with no other reading. B-05 is a degenerate case where all three distractors are off-class. The items that escape both templates (A-02, B-03, B-06, C-02, D-02, D-03) are the batch's strongest. My cold answers matched the key on 24 of 24, consistent with the items being exclusive but also with the templates being learnable.
